title: Your name, the best beginning
intro: Nezami of Ganja (about 1141–1209), in today's Azerbaijan, wrote five long verse romances, the *Khamse* ('Quintet'), which every later Persian storyteller tried to equal. *Leyli and Majnun* (1188) retells an Arab legend. Qeys falls in love with his schoolmate Leyli; the whole tribe talks of it, and her family keeps her from him. He loses his mind with love and wanders the desert among the wild animals, and people call him Majnun, 'the possessed'. Leyli is married against her will to another man but stays faithful to Majnun; they meet only rarely and never live together. When Leyli dies of grief, Majnun comes to her grave and dies there. Like all of Nezami's poems, it begins with a hymn to God; these are its first couplets.

lines.fa: ای نام تو بهترین سرآغاز / بی‌نام تو نامه کی کنم باز
lines.r: ey nām-e to behtarin sar-āghāz / bi-nām-e to nāme key konam bāz
lines.en: O you whose name is the best of beginnings, / how could I open a book without your name?

lines.fa: ای یاد تو مونس روانم / جز نام تو نیست بر زبانم
lines.r: ey yād-e to munes-e ravān-am / joz nām-e to nist bar zabān-am
lines.en: O you whose memory keeps my soul company, / there is nothing on my tongue but your name.

lines.fa: ای کارگشای هر چه هستند / نام تو کلید هر چه بستند
lines.r: ey kār-goshā-ye har che hastand / nām-e to kelid-e har che bastand
lines.en: O you who open the way for all that exists, / your name is the key to all that is locked.
words: one who opens the way, solves problems (lit. 'work-opener')

lines.fa: ای هیچ خطی نگشته ز اول / بی‌حجت نام تو مسجل
lines.r: ey hich khatti nagashte ze avval / bi-hojjat-e nām-e to mosajjal
lines.en: O you without whose name as warrant / no document has been valid since the beginning.
lines.note: The image is a legal document: nothing is valid until it carries your name as its seal.

lines.fa: ای هست کن اساس هستی / کوته ز درت دراز دستی
lines.r: ey hast kon-e asās-e hasti / kute ze dar-at derāz dasti
lines.en: O you who brought the foundation of being into being, / at your door the long arm of the mighty falls short.
lines.note: «دست‌درازی» 'long-handedness' is still the Persian for grabbing what is not yours, or for aggression.
words: maker of being, the one who says 'Be!'

lines.fa: ای خطبه‌ی تو تبارک الله / فیض تو همیشه بارک الله
lines.r: ey khotbe-ye to tabārak allāh / feyz-e to hamishe bārak allāh
lines.en: O you whose sermon is 'Blessed be God', / whose grace is forever 'God bless it'.
lines.note: بارک‌الله *bārakallāh* is still how Iranians say 'well done!', especially to children.

lines.fa: ای هفت عروس نه عماری / بر درگه تو به پرده‌داری
lines.r: ey haft 'arus-e noh 'amāri / bar dargah-e to be parde-dāri
lines.en: O you at whose door the seven brides in their nine litters / stand as keepers of the curtain.
lines.note: In the old astronomy the seven planets ride through nine nested spheres; here they are brides in litters who serve as doorkeepers at God's court.
words: the seven brides – the seven planets
nine (not نه na 'no') – the nine heavenly spheres
a litter carried on a camel or an elephant
keeping the curtain – serving as a chamberlain

lines.fa: ای واهب عقل و باعث جان / با حکم تو هست و نیست یکسان
lines.r: ey vāheb-e 'aghl o bā'es-e jān / bā hokm-e to hast o nist yeksān
lines.en: O giver of reason and raiser of the soul, / before your command, being and not-being are the same.
lines.note: This couplet and the next come from a little further on in the hymn; a few couplets in between are left out here.
words: cause, the one who brings about (Arabic)
what is and what is not

lines.fa: ای محرم عالم تحیر / عالم ز تو هم تهی و هم پر
lines.r: ey mahram-e 'ālam-e tahayyor / 'ālam ze to ham tohi vo ham por
lines.en: O you who are at home in the world of bewilderment, / the world is both empty of you and full of you.

commentary:
**The images.** Every couplet begins with [[ای|ey]] 'O you…', and each gives God a new title taken from ordinary life. He is the opening without which no book can begin, the companion of the soul, the key to every lock, the seal that makes a document valid, a door at which the mighty are powerless, a court where the planets wait as chamberlains. The last couplet turns to paradox, as mystical poetry loves to do: the world is empty of God, because he cannot be seen in it, and full of him, because everything comes from him. For a poem about a lover who loses himself completely in the beloved, it is a fitting beginning.

**The rhythm.** *Leyli and Majnun* is in a short, light metre (*hazaj*): *DUM-DUM-da da-DUM-da-DUM da-DUM-DUM*. Read *ey nā-me to beh-ta-rin sar-ā-ghāz*. Nezami made it the classic metre for the story: Jami and many later poets used it for their own versions of Leyli and Majnun. Each couplet rhymes on its own, sometimes with a repeated word after the rhyme: [[هستند|hastand]] / [[بستند|bastand]], [[تبارک الله|tabārak allāh]] / [[بارک الله|bārak allāh]].

**The grammar.** The hymn is built on one structure, [[ای|ey]] + a description of God, and there are almost no verbs, because [[است|ast]] 'is' is understood: [[ای یاد تو مونس روانم|ey yād-e to munes-e ravān-am]] is 'O you (whose) memory (is) the companion of my soul'. [[ز|ze]] is [[از|az]], [[کوته|kute]] is [[کوتاه|kutāh]], [[درگه|dargah]] is [[درگاه|dargāh]], and [[نگشته|nagashte]] is [[نشده|nashode]]. The first couplet in modern prose: [[ای خدایی که نامت بهترین آغاز است، بی‌نام تو چطور نامه‌ای را باز کنم؟|ey khodāyi ke nām-at behtarin āghāz ast, bi nām-e to chetowr nāme-i rā bāz konam?]]

**Using it.** [[ای نام تو بهترین سرآغاز|ey nām-e to behtarin sar-āghāz]] is often written at the top of a first page – of a book, a speech or a school essay – and it is one of the first couplets of classical poetry many Iranians learn. [[کارگشا|kār-goshā]] 'that gets things done' and [[دست‌درازی|dast-derāzi]] 'aggression' are still everyday words, and [[بارک‌الله|bārakallāh]] is what an Iranian teacher says to a pupil who gets it right.
